1.title: the words before every beginning
1.hook: the words before every beginning — a meal, a drive, an exam
1.tomorrow: what your prayer is actually saying
1.howItsDone: Muslims say bismillah before eating, drinking, setting out, studying and many small daily tasks, and the full line, bismillah ar-rahman ar-rahim, is recited before reading the Qur'an.

segments.voice: Before the first bite of dinner. Before the car pulls out of the driveway. At the top of an exam, before the first answer. Under the breath, fast, so it's easy to miss: bismillah. Many Muslims have said it since before they could read. It goes before a beginning, so it goes first here too. First, a guess.
screen: `BEFORE THE FIRST BITE.` → `BEFORE THE CAR PULLS OUT.` → `BISMILLAH.`

segments.voice: Bismillah is three pieces. Bi: in, or with. Ism: name. Allah: God. In the name of God. Allah isn't the name of a separate god; it's the Arabic word for God, and Arabic-speaking Christians and Jews say it too. The full line is bismillah ar-rahman ar-rahim: “In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful.” All but one of the Qur'an's chapters, called surahs, open with it. So what does it do? Starting in someone's name means you're not starting alone. It's like working under a name you respect: the work carries that name now, so you want it to be worth carrying. That's why it goes before small things, not only big ones. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ once told a boy eating beside him: say bismillah, and eat with your right hand. And for the times you forget, because everyone does, another of his sayings gives a way back in: say it when you remember, in the name of God, at its beginning and its end. Nobody gets locked out of their own lunch.
screen: `BI — IN. ISM — NAME. ALLAH — GOD.` · `ALL BUT ONE SURAH OPENS WITH IT.` · `YOU'RE NOT STARTING ALONE.` · `FORGOT? SAY IT WHEN YOU REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. Think of the very next thing you'll do after this: coffee, an email, the car. Breathe in. On the way out, say the word for it, aloud or under your breath: bismillah. Or simply give it one full pause before it begins.
Bismillah. In the name of God: the words before a beginning, so nothing starts alone. First word on your strand.
screen: `BISMILLAH — your 1st word` → clicks onto an empty word-strand.

segments.voice: Your line: start in the name of. It's why the word comes before a meal, a drive, an exam, and why it came first here. See you tomorrow.

2.title: what your prayer is actually saying
2.hook: seven verses said in every prayer, many times a day, and what they actually say
2.carry: a conversation, answered line by line
2.howItsDone: Muslims recite al-Fatiha in Arabic in every unit of every prayer, and at many other moments: over the sick, at a wedding, for someone who has died. Many learn it as children, before any other surah.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bismillah, in the name of God. Today, the prayer that opens with it.

It's said in every unit of every prayer: seventeen times on an ordinary day. Many Muslims learned it by heart as children and could say it half asleep. Ask what it means, line by line, and a lot of people go quiet. There's a question people really ask: what's the point of praying in Arabic if I don't understand it? Today, the whole thing, in plain English.
screen: `SEVENTEEN TIMES A DAY.` → `WHAT DOES IT SAY?` → `IN PLAIN ENGLISH.`

segments.voice: It's called al-Fatiha, the opening: the first surah of the Qur'an, from a root meaning to open. A key, in Arabic, is a miftah. Seven short verses. Here they are, in plain words. In the name of God, the Beneficent, the Merciful. Praise be to God, Lord of the Worlds. The Beneficent, the Merciful. Owner of the Day of Judgment. You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help. Show us the straight path: the path of those You have favored, not of those who earn anger, nor of those who go astray. That's all of it. Notice the shape. It opens in yesterday's name. Then praise, and mercy said twice. Then it turns from talking about God to talking to God: You. And when it finally asks for something, it asks for one thing. Not money, not health. Directions. A saying the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ reported from God describes it as a conversation. When someone praying says, praise be to God, Lord of the Worlds, God answers: My servant has praised Me. Line after line, an answer comes back. So here's the answer to the Arabic question. The words don't change. Knowing them changes how you say them. Even one line, known while you say it, gives a wandering mind somewhere to stand.
screen: `AL-FATIHA — THE OPENING.` · `SEVEN VERSES, IN PLAIN ENGLISH.` · `PRAISE FIRST, THEN ONE REQUEST.` · `A CONVERSATION, ANSWERED.`

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. Breathe in. On the way out, say the one request, in Arabic or in English: ihdina s-sirat al-mustaqim. Show us the straight path. It's the line the whole prayer leans toward.
Al-Fatiha. The opening: seven verses, praise first, then one request. Second word on your strand.
Your line: a conversation, answered line by line. Next time you hear it, you'll know what's being said. Day two, done.

3.title: the water before the words
3.hook: washing before prayer: why these parts, in this order
3.howItsDone: Muslims make wudu before prayer unless they are still in a state of wudu from an earlier washing; mosques have washing areas with taps, and at home it's done at an ordinary sink.

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-Fatiha, a conversation, answered line by line. Today, what comes before a single word of it.

Near the door of many mosques there's a row of taps along a wall, a low ledge to sit on, a drain along the floor. Before the prayer, people stop here first. Sleeves up, shoes off. Water over the hands, into the mouth, over the face, up the arms, over the feet. If you grew up with it, you could do it with your eyes closed. So: why these parts, and why this order?
screen: `A ROW OF TAPS BY THE DOOR.` → `HANDS, FACE, ARMS, FEET.` → `WHY THESE? WHY THIS ORDER?`

segments.voice: It's called wudu, from a root with the sense of brightness, the way a washed face shines. The core is one verse of the Qur'an: “When ye rise up for prayer, wash your faces, and your hands up to the elbows,” then wipe the head, and then the feet. Face, arms, head, feet: that's the order, and it comes from the verse itself. The rest, the hands first, the mouth and nose, the ears, families learned from the way the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ showed his companions. Here's the surprising part. It isn't really about dirt. People make wudu when they're already clean. A saying of the Prophet pictures it this way: as the water runs off your face, the wrongs your eyes looked at run off with it; off the hands, what the hands did; off the feet, where the feet went. So it's a reset, done with the body: the step between the street and the prayer. It lasts until something breaks it, like sleep, so it isn't always a fresh wash for every prayer. And when there's no water, or water would harm you, the same verse allows clean earth instead. That's called tayammum. The reset is never out of reach.
screen: `WUDU — FROM A ROOT OF BRIGHTNESS.` · `FACE, ARMS, HEAD, FEET.` · `THE WRONGS RUN OFF WITH THE WATER.` · `NO WATER? CLEAN EARTH.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. If there's water near you, wash your hands slowly and feel it run off your fingers. If not, rest your hands open and picture cool water over them, then over your face. With each breath out, let one thing from today run off with it.
Wudu. The washing before prayer: face, arms, head and feet. A reset with water. Third word.
Your line: rinse the day off. The day doesn't have to come with you into the prayer. Day three.

4.title: inshallah or mashallah?
4.hook: two words people mix up: one looks ahead, one looks at what's already here
4.carry: inshallah for tomorrow, mashallah for today
4.howItsDone: Muslims add inshallah, "if God wills," when they speak of something they intend to do, following Qur'an 18:23–24, and say mashallah, "what God has willed," when they see or hear of something good: a new baby, good news, something beautiful.

segments.voice: Yesterday: wudu, a reset with water. Today, two words that get mixed up all the time.

See you tomorrow? Inshallah. Will the report be done by Friday? Inshallah. A cousin's new baby, a friend's new apartment, a kid's first goal: mashallah. They sound alike, they both have Allah in them, and people swap them around, Muslims included. There's even a family joke that inshallah is the politest way to say probably not. The real difference fits in one line.
screen: `SEE YOU TOMORROW? INSHALLAH.` → `A NEW BABY? MASHALLAH.` → `WHAT'S THE DIFFERENCE?`

segments.voice: In sha' Allah: if God wills. It looks ahead, at something that hasn't happened yet. It comes from the eighteenth surah of the Qur'an, the Cave: “And say not of anything: Lo! I shall do that tomorrow, Except if Allah will.” So it isn't maybe. Maybe is about your mood. Inshallah is about what you don't control. You plan completely, and admit that tomorrow isn't yours to hand out. It was never a reason to skip the work, either. A man once asked the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ whether he should leave his camel untied and trust God. Tie it, came the answer, and trust. Now its twin. Ma sha' Allah: what God has willed. It looks at something good that's already here: a baby, a new job, a view that stops you. It says, this is a gift, not only my doing. And it comes from the same surah. A few verses on, a man walks proudly through his gardens, and his friend asks why he didn't say, on the way in, what God wills. So: inshallah for tomorrow. Mashallah for what's already here.
screen: `INSHALLAH — IF GOD WILLS.` · `TIE YOUR CAMEL, AND TRUST.` · `MASHALLAH — WHAT GOD HAS WILLED.` · `SAME SURAH, TWO DIRECTIONS.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, think of one thing you've planned for tomorrow. On the second, notice the part of it that's up to you, and the part that isn't. On the third, think of one good thing already in your life, and let it be a gift.
Inshallah. If God wills: a real plan, held with an open hand. And its twin, mashallah, for what's already here. Fourth word.
Your line: inshallah for tomorrow, mashallah for today. That's the whole difference. That's day four.

story.title: the man with two gardens
story.text: A man owns two gardens heavy with grapes, ringed with date palms, a stream running between them. Walking through them with a friend, he says he can't imagine any of it ever ending. His friend asks him: when you came in, why didn't you say, what God wills; there is no strength except in God? Then the harvest is struck down, and the man is left wringing his hands over everything he spent on it.

5.title: is doubt okay?
5.hook: the question people type late at night: is it haram to doubt?
5.carry: ask, so the heart can rest
5.howItsDone: Muslims speak of iman, faith, as something that grows and weakens over a life; many bring their questions to a teacher, an imam or a study circle, and the Qur'an and hadith are often read for answers to doubt.

segments.voice: Yesterday: inshallah for tomorrow, mashallah for today. Today, a question many people only ever ask a search bar.

It's late, the phone is the only light in the room, and someone types a question they'd never ask out loud: is it haram to doubt your faith? A question from a class that won't go away. A stretch when prayer felt empty. Underneath it is one worry: if I have questions, am I still in? Before any rule, this path starts there, because the oldest answers are gentler than people expect.
screen: `LATE AT NIGHT, ONE QUESTION.` → `IS IT HARAM TO DOUBT?` → `AM I STILL IN?`

segments.voice: Start with the word for faith: iman. Its root, a-m-n, is the root of safety and of trust; the same root gives amana, something entrusted to you. So iman is less a certificate you hold and more a trust you live in. The Qur'an even speaks of believers adding faith to their faith, as if it can grow. That's why people say my iman is low when prayer goes dry for a while: a faith that can grow can also dip, and come back. Now the question. Some of the Prophet Muhammad's ﷺ companions once came to him, troubled. We find thoughts in ourselves, they said, so bad we can hardly bring ourselves to say them. Do you really find that? he asked. Yes. That, he said, is clear faith. Not the thought itself: being troubled by it. Their discomfort showed how much they cared. And the Qur'an tells of a prophet who asked. Ibrahim, Abraham, says: my Lord, show me how You give life to the dead. Don't you believe? comes the reply. And he answers: “Yea, but (I ask) in order that my heart may be at ease.” He isn't scolded. He's shown. Scholars have a lot to say about the difference between a passing question and turning away, and this path will get there. For today, the plain part: in these stories, asking is a way of looking for rest. And if a late-night question ever comes with real darkness, the kind where you can't see a way through, please reach out tonight: 988 in the US, or local emergency help.
screen: `IMAN — FROM A ROOT OF SAFETY AND TRUST.` · `THAT IS CLEAR FAITH.` · `SHOW ME, SO MY HEART MAY BE AT EASE.` · `ASKING, TO FIND REST.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, let one honest question come up, whatever it is. On the second, don't answer it; just hold it, the way Ibrahim held his. On the third, breathe out, and let your heart rest a moment, with the question still open.
Iman. Faith: from a root of safety and trust, a faith that can grow, with room for questions. Fifth word.
Your line: ask, so the heart can rest. Ibrahim asked, and he wasn't turned away. Day five, done.

6.title: one day of Ramadan
6.hook: a kitchen at four in the morning: one day of the fast, from suhoor to iftar
6.howItsDone: During Ramadan, adult Muslims who are able fast from dawn to sunset, eat a pre-dawn meal called suhoor, break the fast at sunset with iftar, often with dates and water, and many mosques hold extra night prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: iman, a faith with room to ask. Today, a month many Muslims know from the inside, told start to finish.

Four in the morning, and the kitchen light is on. A family, half asleep, eating dates and eggs and drinking as much water as they can before the sky starts to pale. Then, from dawn, nothing: no food, not even a sip of water, until sunset. If you grew up with it, you know every hour of that day. It's rarely told start to finish, with what it's for. So here's one day.
screen: `A KITCHEN AT FOUR IN THE MORNING.` → `THEN NOTHING UNTIL SUNSET.` → `ONE DAY, START TO FINISH.`

segments.voice: Ramadan is a month of the Islamic calendar, which follows the moon, so it slides earlier every year and passes through every season. Here's one day of it. Before dawn, suhoor, the early meal. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said there's a blessing in it, so people eat even when they'd rather sleep. At first light comes the dawn prayer, and the fast begins: no food, no drink, until sunset. That's the fourth pillar, sawm. Then the day itself: work, school, errands, and a hunger that keeps tapping you on the shoulder. Here's what it's for. The Qur'an says it plainly: “Fasting is prescribed for you, even as it was prescribed for those before you, that ye may ward off (evil).” The word underneath is taqwa, a careful awareness. The hunger is a tool, not the point. Another of the Prophet's sayings makes that sharp: whoever doesn't give up lying, God has no need of their giving up food and drink. At sunset, iftar: the fast breaks, often with a date and water, the way the Prophet broke his. And it's built for real people: the sick and travelers are excused, and make the days up later. Why this month? The Qur'an names it as the month the Qur'an was revealed.

Ramadan. The month of the fast, dawn to sunset, and the month the Qur'an was revealed. Sixth word.

story.title: the cave above Mecca
story.text: A man alone in a mountain cave above Mecca, where he often went to be by himself, suddenly isn't alone. Someone grips him tight and gives one command: read. I am not a reader, he says. The grip tightens again, and again, and then come the first words of the Qur'an. He runs home shaking and says to his wife, Khadijah: cover me, cover me. Tradition places that night in Ramadan.

7.title: two Eids, not one
7.hook: new clothes, an envelope from an uncle, and the second Eid people forget
7.tomorrow: the greeting that is a wish
7.howItsDone: On both Eids Muslims gather in the morning for the Eid prayer, dress in their best, visit family, share food and greet each other with Eid Mubarak; children often get gifts of money. Before Eid al-Fitr each household gives zakat al-fitr, and at Eid al-Adha those able offer an animal and share the meat.

segments.voice: Yesterday: one day of Ramadan, dark to dark. Six words so far: bismillah, al-Fatiha, wudu, inshallah, iman, Ramadan. Today, the seventh.

The morning after Ramadan ends, kids are up early in new clothes. An uncle hands out envelopes of money. The family heads to a prayer held in the morning, and then it's visits, sweets, and Eid Mubarak said so many times it blurs. And yet plenty of people, Muslims included, half forget there's a second Eid a couple of months later, or what makes it different. Today, both.
screen: `NEW CLOTHES. AN ENVELOPE.` → `EID MUBARAK.` → `AND A SECOND EID.`

segments.voice: Eid is tied to a root meaning to return: a day that comes back around, every year. When the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ arrived in Medina, a saying reports, people there had two old days of games and celebration. God has given you two better ones, he told them: the day of breaking the fast, and the day of sacrifice. The first is Eid al-Fitr. Fitr means breaking the fast. It closes Ramadan, and before the Eid prayer, each household gives a small gift of food, zakat al-fitr, so people in need can celebrate too. The second is Eid al-Adha, the feast of sacrifice. It falls during the hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca, and it remembers Ibrahim, Abraham, and the ram given in place of his son. Families who are able offer an animal, and share the meat with relatives, neighbors and people in need. So one Eid closes a month of fasting, and the other comes with the pilgrimage. Both begin with a prayer, and both are built so nobody is left out of the feast. And Eid Mubarak? A blessed Eid.

story.title: the dream and the ram
story.text: An old man tells his young son something terrible: I've seen in a dream that I must sacrifice you. What do you think? The son doesn't run. Father, he says, do what you've been told; God willing, you'll find me patient. As the father lays him down, a voice calls out: you've already fulfilled the vision. A great sacrifice is given in the boy's place.
